title: 14 Tips Toward Better Relationships with Administrators, Parents, & Support Staff
author: Dave Stuart Jr.
summary: In the closing installment of a series on teacher impact, Dave Stuart Jr. offers practical advice for working well with the non-colleague adults in a school: administrators, parents and support staff. With administrators, he urges a mastery rather than performance orientation toward evaluation, reading each administrator's appetite for candid feedback, handling discipline in one's own room rather than sending students to the office, and assuming good motives. With parents, he recommends crediting them as the key players in their child's life, making positive phone calls, and explaining a grading and management system grounded in growth and grit. With support staff, he insists on their dignity regardless of job performance, illustrated by a former principal who quietly picked up hallway trash. The post closes by reducing all of this to one question: whether a teacher comes to school to be served or to serve.
points: Obsessing over evaluation points rather than mastery of the craft is named as the thing that reliably poisons a teacher's relationship with an administrator, and building financial cushion is suggested as a way to loosen that grip.
Teachers should diagnose whether their administrator welcomes straight talk or prefers role distance, and adjust accordingly rather than relying on others' opinions.
Stuart tells parents they, not he, are the biggest factor in their child's development, and frames his class around college-and-career readiness plus one year's growth in character.
A grading system that allows revision and late work with small penalties is presented as a way to show parents that both academics and character matter.
Support staff must be treated as dignified human beings whose worth is not set by job performance, modeled by a principal who quietly picked up hallway garbage.
quotes: But, like a college professor once said to me, we've got to act as teachers as if we're not afraid to lose our jobs. This isn't license to act a fool; it is encouragement to be about mastering this work rather than simply performing well in an eval.

So do yourself a favor: start making baby steps toward having an emergency fund, toward living on less, etc. — do what you can to move those financial pieces into place — so that you can worry less about points and more about becoming great at the job. This won't just help you work better with administrators; it'll decrease your stress!
The key is this, however: figure out which kind of administrator yours is. Some will respect you speaking truth to power; others will not appreciate it.

At the end of the day, humility would lead us to assume that our administrators aren't the caricatures we often make them out to be (remember: consider others better than yourselves). I try to remind myself that you couldn't pay me enough to be an administrator; they are simultaneously balancing the needs and desires of teachers, students, parents, the school board, the superintendent… I'd be a different person if I was under that kind of pressure. So even when an administrator behaves poorly, I try to assume that her or his intention isn't bad — they're simply human.

So the point here is that I want parents to understand I'm not some dragon up in the ivory tower with an arbitrary grading system, and at the same time I'm not a loosey-goosey grader. There's a central logic to my grading system, and it is that academics and character matter.

Whenever Scriven was walking down a hallway, if he saw some garbage on the ground he'd bend over and pick it up. I think that's a simple, important way we can remind ourselves, physically, that we're not above any task that will make our school a better place.
Too often, we forget that our building support staffs interact with students frequently throughout their day. With that in mind, it's important to remember to be encouraging toward them as well.
